questions.text: What distinguishes Tree-of-Thought from a single linear Chain-of-Thought?

options.A: It samples complete solutions and votes on their final answers.
options.B: It selects similar demonstrations before generating a single solution.
options.C: It evaluates partial reasoning branches and expands promising candidates.
options.D: It splits work into a fixed sequence without comparing alternatives.

questions.explanation: Tree-of-Thought searches over candidate partial solutions, evaluates them, and expands promising branches.

questions.text: A question-answering task needs facts available only through an external search tool. Which approach directly incorporates retrieved observations into subsequent decisions?

options.A: Few-shot prompting with a fixed set of labeled demonstrations.
options.B: ReAct with repeated action, observation, and decision steps.
options.C: Self-consistency with voting over answers generated without tools.
options.D: A longer single reasoning trace generated without external actions.

questions.explanation: ReAct incorporates tool observations into the next reasoning and action decisions.

questions.text: In the lesson voting code, five samples yield extracted answers ["24", None, "24", None, "27"]. None values are discarded before confidence is computed as winning votes / len(answers). What are the winning answer and confidence?

options.A: "24" and 2/5, because all requested samples form the denominator.
options.B: "27" and 1/3, because the last valid answer wins the vote.
options.C: None and 0, because any extraction failure invalidates the result.
options.D: "24" and 2/3, because only extracted answers form the denominator.

questions.explanation: The code retains three parsed answers; two vote for "24". Its confidence ignores extraction failures and is not a calibrated probability of correctness.
